field_group: Common annual or winter-annual pioneer aster/horseweed
look_here_first: LOOK HERE FIRST: SEASONAL SEQUENCE. (1) Autumn/winter flat rosette of elongated, often unevenly TOOTHED lower leaves; (2) one erect leafy stem with many NARROW, ALTERNATE, sessile stem leaves, smaller toward tip; (3) large upper panicle of numerous TINY greenish capitula, with an involucre ~3–4 mm LONG and rays usually too short to see without a hand lens; (4) white fluffy pappus as fruits mature. Compare a rooted plant and actual flowering heads before confirming an ambiguous rosette. No bright yellow goldenrod plume.
project_tracker_diagnostic: Annual/winter-annual taproot and lower toothed rosette; one upright leafy stem with progressively smaller alternate narrow blades; strongly branched terminal panicle; green phyllary cup/involucre ~3–4 mm LONG; minute pale ray florets; white pappus when fruiting.

morphology_keys.life_cycle: Annual or winter annual, commonly from a small taproot, overwintering flat rosette before bolting; not a long-lived basal clump.
morphology_keys.basal: Early leaves spatulate to oblanceolate, often shallow teeth, up to ~10 cm; basal leaves often shrivel as plant flowers.
morphology_keys.stem: One generally straight, unbranched lower stem, leafy with many narrow alternate sessile leaves. Branches concentrated near the TOP in a loose tapering panicle (not grass spike or yellow goldenrod raceme).
morphology_keys.leaves: Alternate, linear to narrowly oblanceolate, lower 20–50(-100) × 4–10(-15) mm, upper progressively narrower, edges sometimes toothed or ciliate with stiff marginal hairs; surfaces often almost smooth except veins.
morphology_keys.heads: Many tiny heads in a terminal panicle; the INVOLUCRE (the bract cup beneath one head) is about 3–4 mm LONG, not necessarily a 3–4 mm diameter for the full head. Marginal very short white or pinkish ray-floret tips ~0.5–1 mm usually hard to see without magnification; central tubular florets present. Distinguish fresh flowers from ripe silky pappus.
morphology_keys.fruit: Dry one-seeded cypsela ~1–1.5 mm with one ring of fine white pappus bristles usually ~2–3 mm; wind distributed.
morphology_keys.site: Disturbed open ground, roadsides, empty beds, old fields, turf gaps, margins. Disturbance-tolerant early successional plant, but not by itself a determination of native-zone certification.
morphology_keys.variation: Flower heads and stems vary with age, drought and site; non-native-looking labels on overseas photographs describe local status abroad, not species' North American origin.
best_field_traits: narrow ALTERNATE stem leaves and single central stem
pyramid of MANY very small whitish heads (not a yellow display)
white fuzzy pappus after seed maturation

comparisons.key_distinctions: On a mature plant, horseweed usually has ONE tall leafy axis, many narrow ALTERNATE leaves, and scores of tiny terminal heads (involucre ~3–4 mm long) with barely projecting whitish ray florets. E. strigosus, E. philadelphicus and E. annuus typically present fewer, larger, clearly daisy-like heads with visible projecting rays; a rosette alone is not a confident separation. E. geiseri is annual but has visibly longer fleabane rays; E. modestus has a woody perennial root crown. Goldenrods (Solidago) have conspicuous yellow rays in yellow flowering sprays. Similar small-headed Conyza/Erigeron bonariensis/sumatrensis should be keyed with hair and phyllary detail; their occurrence here is not asserted.

photo_diagnostic_lesson.title: Horseweed: learn all four seasons/stages

steps.text: Low spatulate/oblanceolate leaves with irregular shallow teeth. Photograph full leaf and plant base. Other little rosettes nearby can be DIFFERENT species; rosette alone rarely enough.
One tall upright stem with many alternate slender leaves; lower leaves broader and toothed, upper leaves narrower and mostly entire. Small hairs may fringe leaves or stem.

steps.look: Head is NOT a big daisy
steps.text: A hand lens should show extremely short white to pale pink marginal ray florets around the tiny head; the enclosing green INVOLUCRE is roughly 3–4 mm long. CURRENT SITE PHOTOS DO NOT SHOW OPEN FRESH RAYS: the two existing macros are fruiting. Photograph a live flowering head at scale to confirm.
Fruit heads open to release tiny dry cypselae with fine, whitish PAPPUS bristles for wind dispersal. The two installed close-ups show this stage, not open fresh florets.

glossary.rosette: Flat basal arrangement of leaves before flower stalk develops
glossary.bolting: Rapid growth of flower-bearing stem from earlier basal stage
glossary.alternate: ONE leaf at a node, next leaf at another level on opposite side
glossary.capitulum: One tiny composite flower head, made of many minute florets
glossary.ray_floret: Small strap-tipped flower at head edge; horseweed's rays are barely visible
glossary.pappus: Fine bristles atop the small dry fruit that help it float
glossary.phyllary: One of the small bracts forming the green involucre/cup under a composite head
glossary.cypsela: One-seeded dry fruit of the aster family

photo_diagnostic_lesson.memory_rule: ROSETTE → ONE LEAFY STICK → MANY TINY FLOWER HEADS → WHITE FLUFF. Use alternate leaves and scale; no guessing a rosette or confusing seed fluff for petals.

items.label: WINTER ROSETTE — HORSEWEED VS NEARBY OTHER ROSETTE
items.caption: The LARGE gray-green rosette with elongated, unevenly toothed leaves is horseweed; the small green rosette below-left is a DIFFERENT PLANT (Draba verna). Follow the horseweed leaf margins and crown. Source photographed in Poland, not Hays County.
items.creator: Agnieszka Kwiecień, Nova
items.annotation_status: Image visually inspected: large horseweed rosette and separate smaller Draba confirmed; three overlays point to visible parts; owner mobile arrow check pending.
items.why_it_matters: Teach the crew to trace leaves to one crown before assigning an ID. Winter rosettes can overlap in appearance: do not identify the small adjacent Draba as horseweed, and confirm ambiguous horseweed rosettes after bolting.

items.label: BOLTED PLANT — ALTERNATE LEAVES AND TERMINAL BRANCHING
items.caption: A SINGLE tall central axis bears many NARROW alternate leaves, with many more branchlets and tiny heads near the top. The tall image does not expose the taproot; do not infer it from the photograph.
items.creator: Rasbak
items.annotation_status: Image visually inspected at full portrait scale; arrow tips placed on terminal head cluster, attached leaf, and upright stem; owner mobile arrow check pending.
items.why_it_matters: The combination of alternate narrow stem leaves, one dominant erect axis, and many small upper heads is a much stronger field clue than height alone.

items.label: OPEN FRUITING HEAD — PAPPUS, NOT FRESH BLOOMS
items.caption: IMPORTANT STAGE CORRECTION: this macro shows a head already in the FRUITING/dispersal stage, with abundant spread-out white pappus bristles and an exposed spent head center. It does NOT prove the tiny white fresh ray florets, despite the source filename containing 'flowerhead'.
items.creator: Rasbak
items.annotation_status: Source JPEG pixel-inspected 2026-10-20. Reclassified from inaccurately labeled flower macro to pappus-stage macro; neither ray florets nor a scale bar is visible. Two verified visible-target arrow coordinates; mobile check pending.
items.why_it_matters: Do not teach the silky fruiting bristles as petals. A separate actual blooming close-up with a millimeter scale is still required.

items.label: OLDER SEED HEAD — FEATHERY FRUIT DISPERSAL
items.caption: A later fruiting head has fine WHITE PAPPUS BRISTLES spread around pale spent florets and mature fruits. The broad green foreground leaf is not labeled horseweed because its plant attachment/identity is not verifiable from this crop.
items.creator: Rasbak
items.annotation_status: Original source visually inspected: pappus and central fruiting cluster visible; foreground leaf not used as a diagnostic character; owner mobile arrow check pending.
items.why_it_matters: Learn the transition from a compact composite head into light wind-dispersal fluff, but confirm species with intact leaves and flowering/fruiting architecture.

field_id_finalization.lesson_goal: Crew can follow the same species from basal rosette through bolting to fine seeded heads, identify a different adjacent rosette and distinguish fleabane/goldenrod look-alikes.
field_id_finalization.five_second_field_rule: Toothed low rosette? Follow it later. Taller single leafy stick with ALTERNATE narrow leaves and hundreds of very small terminal heads? Horseweed likely. Tiny pale rays need a hand lens. Late fluffy pappus is not flower petals.

compare_in_field.first_check: Larger daisy-like heads with obvious protruding white/pink/lavender rays rather than horseweed's tiny nearly rayless-looking heads.
compare_in_field.caution: Rosette-only plants can overlap; head characters needed.

compare_in_field.first_check: Typically broader, more coarsely toothed lower leaves and showier rayed heads; confirm flowering plant.
compare_in_field.caution: Not a guaranteed leaf-only split; check the flowerhead.

compare_in_field.first_check: Also an annual slender-taproot fleabane but has notably longer rays, often ~3–6 mm, rather than horseweed's ~0.5–1 mm; check mature head.
compare_in_field.caution: Do not describe E. geiseri as a perennial; its species card documents annual root.

compare_in_field.first_check: Woody persistent root crown and showier heads rather than horseweed's annually produced tall leafy stem.
compare_in_field.caution: Roots may be inaccessible; compare flowering and stem structure as well.

compare_in_field.first_check: Showy golden-yellow composite heads vs pale inconspicuous horseweed rays.
compare_in_field.caution: Inflorescence outline alone can be misleading, especially before bloom.
